units.la: AMPLISSIMO ET CLA-RISSIMO VIRO DN. NICOLAO DOBBINO, I. V. DOCTORI PRAE-stantissimo, Electoralis Palatinatus Consiliario intimo & dignissimo, Domino ac Patrono plurimum colendo.
units.tr: TO THE MOST DISTINGUISHED AND ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, MR. NICOLAUS DOBBINUS, DOCTOR OF BOTH LAWS, OUTSTANDING, THE MOST WORTHY PRIVY COUNSELLOR OF THE ELECTORATE OF THE PALATINATE, MY LORD AND PATRON MOST TO BE HONOURED.

units.la: TANTA gratitudinis & dignitas & efficacitas est: Vir Amplissime, Domine ac Patrone plurimum obseruande: ut vel mutae etiam brutaeq; pecudes, sine ullo rationis discursu, solo naturae instinctu, ob generisui conseruationē hāc virtutē penè æmulari, & non sine magna quan-doque admiratione imitari videantur; velut ex A. Gellij, Aeliani, Appionis Po-lyhistoris, Fulgosi, Egnatij, & aliorum, historia, quin etiam è communi expe-rientia, liquidò peruidere promptum est. Perquàm ergo scitè & eleganter M. ille Tullius in oratione pro Planco: Cùm omnibus, ait, virtutibus me asse-ctum esse cupiam, tum nihil est, quod malim tamen, quàm me gratum & esse & videri: Hæc enim est una virtus, non solùm maxima, sed etiam mater virtu-tum reliquarum. Quæ cùm altius, uti par est, expenderem: facere non potui, Vir Clarissime, quin pro eximia illa erga me tua, quam hactenus expertus sum, benevolentia, aliquo modo gratum me exhiberem, aut aliquam saltem animi grati significationem ostenderem. Sed cum aliud hoc tempore non esset in promptu, quod Excellētia tua dignum, & studiis meis accommodatum esset: præsentem hanc meam (sic enim appel-lare libuit) Philosophicæ Festivitatis Pa-negyrim; quam crebra studiosorum in-terpellatione, & amicorum exhortatio-ne permotus, in publicum exire passus sum; Amplissimo Nomini tuo inscri-bere ac dicare volui. Nec immerito. Cùm enim inter alios doctos & ho-nonoratos viros te cum primis ad Fane-gyricam istam Philosophicæ Promo-tionis festiuitatem exoptassemus & in-uitassemus, ita humaniter nos accepi-sti, ita ad petitionem nostram promptus fuisti, vt non modò tuâ nobis exoptatis-simam præsentiam vltrò benignè spon-deres, sed postea quoque cùm ardua & grauissima negocia te à nobis præter opinionem abstraxissent, diligenter te nobis (quæ tua humilitas est) excusares. Mitto igitur ad te leuidense hoc mu-nusculum literarium, Amplissimo No-mini tuo dicatum, meæ erga te obser-uantiæ & gratitudinis testimonium: atque istud æqui bonique; donec Deus meliora; iam consulas; meque & studia mea, vt hactenus, ita porrò ac perpe-tuò tibi fideliter commendata habeas, enixè obsecro. Ego verò isthæc tua me-rita verbis, quibus grauissimis potero, sedulò tollam, vtque eorum memoria apud me & fama intermoriatur, nun-quam admittam. Vale Mecænas, ac bene de me mereri, quod & facis, perge. E museo, Nonis Martij, Anni Christiani MDXC.
units.tr: Such is the worth, dignity and power of gratitude, most distinguished sir, my lord and patron most to be respected, that even dumb and brute beasts, without any process of reason, by the instinct of nature alone, seem almost to emulate this virtue for the preservation of their kind, and sometimes to imitate it with no small admiration. This can readily be seen plainly from the histories of A. Gellius, Aelian, Appian the Polyhistor, Fulgosus, Egnatius and others, and indeed from common experience. Therefore M. Tullius says very neatly and elegantly in his speech for Plancus: "Although I wish to be endowed with all the virtues, there is nothing I would rather be than grateful and seen to be so; for this is one virtue, not only the greatest, but also the mother of the other virtues." When I weighed this more deeply, as is fitting, I could not refrain, most distinguished sir, from showing myself in some way grateful for your outstanding goodwill towards me, which I have experienced until now, or at least from showing some sign of a grateful mind. But since at this time nothing else was at hand that was worthy of your Excellency and suited to my studies, I have wished to inscribe and dedicate to your most distinguished name this present panegyric of my philosophical festivity (for so I have chosen to call it), which I allowed to go out to the public, moved by the frequent entreaties of students and the exhortation of friends. Nor undeservedly. For when we had especially wished for and invited you, among other learned and honoured men, to this panegyric festivity of the philosophical promotion, you received us so kindly and were so ready at our request that not only did you freely and willingly promise us your most desired presence, but afterwards too, when difficult and very weighty affairs drew you away from us contrary to expectation, you diligently excused yourself to us, which is your humility. I therefore send you this light little literary gift, dedicated to your most distinguished name, as a testimony of my respect and gratitude toward you. I earnestly beg you to take it kindly and fairly, until God grants better things, and to hold me and my studies, as hitherto, so also henceforth and forever, faithfully commended to you. For my part, I shall by no means allow your merits to be lost on me, and I will set them forth in words as weighty as I can, so that their memory and fame never die in me. Farewell, Maecenas, and go on to deserve well of me, as indeed you do. From my museum, on the Nones of March, in the Christian year 1590.

units.la: ORATIO DE PRAECIPUIS LAUDIB. ET UTILITATIB. PHILOSOPHIÆ POLITICÆ.
units.tr: An Oration on the Chief Praises and Uses of Political Philosophy.

units.la: Quanquam istas; quas pro isthoc tempore mihi impositas sustineo; partes, haud immerito subterfugere poteram: Magnifice D. Rector, Generosi & Inclyti Domini Barones, Reverendi, Clarissimi, & ornatissimi omnium Facultatum Doctores ac Professores, cæterique genere, doctrina, & eruditione præstantissimi Viri, hospites exoptatissimi, tu denique virtutis ac pietatis, linguarum ac literarum studiosa, & lectissima nobilissimorum ac literatissimorum iuuenum corona: quā-quā istas, aio, quibus nunc defungar, partes, merito renuere ac subterfugere poteram: facit tamen Magnificentiæ, Generositatis, reuerentiæ & humanitatis vestræ (qua me sustento) benignitas: facit eximia venerandi Collegij ac Senatus Philosophici dignitas; meaque Collegis gratificandi facilitas: tui comprimis, Spectatissime Philosophici Ordinis Decane, & ad hunc Actum Procancellarie, D. Doctor Madere, postulati autoritas facit: quin & iustissimæ nouem istorum, quos isthic in medio seorsim locatos spectatis, honestissimorum ac doctissimorum Candidatorum petitionis æquitas facit: Ut in augustam hanc Cathedram ascendere, & laudabile mihi demandatæ provinciæ munus pro virili parte obire; hoc est, nouem illos iam modo renunciatos Philosophiæ Licentiatos supremo Doctoratus seu Magisterij Philosophici honore ac titulo, veIut præclaro modestiæ ac diligentiæ autoramento, & publico virtutis eruditionisque testimonio, solenni veterum ritu, condecorare, non reformidem.
units.tr: Although I could fairly have declined the role I have been given for this occasion, Magnificent Rector, noble and illustrious lords, reverend, distinguished and most accomplished teachers of all the Faculties, and other men most outstanding in rank, learning and erudition, most welcome guests, and finally you, the choice assembly of those devoted to virtue and piety, to languages and letters, and of the most noble and learned young men: I say, I could rightly have refused and avoided the task I am now to perform. Yet your magnificence, dignity, reverence and kindness, on which I rely, has moved me, and the distinguished worth of this venerable College and Philosophical Senate, and my readiness to oblige my colleagues. Above all, the authority of you, most esteemed Dean of the Philosophical Order and Pro-Chancellor for this act, Doctor Madere, has moved me, and the just request of these nine most honourable and learned candidates, whom you see seated apart in the middle. I do not shrink from ascending this venerable chair and, to the best of my ability, discharging the praiseworthy duty assigned to me: that is, from honouring these nine newly named Licentiates of Philosophy with the supreme honour and title of Doctor or Master of Philosophy, in the solemn manner of the ancients, as a distinguished pledge of their modesty and diligence and a public testimony to their virtue and learning.

units.la: Priusquam tamen id facere aggredior, animaduerto majorum nostrorum instituto, promouenti; cuius partes mihi nunc assignatæ; hanc quoque necessitatem incumbere, ut de liberali quodam, id est, & excitandis ad libera-lia virtutum ac literarum studia, liberorum atque ingenuorum animis accommodato, & à proposito nostro haud alieno, & auditu non injucundo, argumento, pauca quædam proœmij loco, antequam Candidatis alteri honores Academici conferantur, præmittam.
units.tr: Before I begin to do so, however, I notice that the custom of our forefathers, which assigns me the part I now have, also requires that, before the other candidates receive their academic honours, I put forward a few introductory remarks on a certain liberal subject, one suited to stirring the minds of free and well-born men towards the liberal studies of virtue and letters, one not foreign to our purpose and not unpleasant to hear.

units.la: Etsi vero alia atque alia præfandi materies sese offert: Sentio tamen non esse mihi nunc quidem integrum, sumere quam velim, sed quam me sumpturum iam pridem receperim. Etenim commemini sse plerosque vestrum arbitror, Auditores, me superiori anno, & hoc ipso fermè tempore, quando Philosophiam Ethicam & Politicam profiteri aggressus sum, ubi de ortu ipsius ac progressu, deque autoribus & cultoribus præfatus essem, polliceri; me, quàm primùm daretur occasio, de veris istarum disci-plinarum laudibus, ac præsertim utilitatibus, ex hoc loco dicturum. Quo equidem argumento vix ullum excogitari nunc quidem posse arbitror, quod vel excitandis ad liberalia virtutis & honestatis, legum & literarum studia, liberorum atque ingenuorum animis accommodatius; vel ad hoc nostrum institutum, ad hoc tempus, ad hunc locum, ad hunc Actum; ubi quippe virtuti, doctrinæ ac modestiæ sua præmia tribuuntur; opportunius, vel auditu denique iucundius, censeri queat. Dicam ergo, fortunante Ieho-va, & temporis ratione habita succinctius dicam, de præcipuo Philosophiæ Politicæ fructu & laudibus: quæ nimirum consistunt in mira eius tum utilitate ac necessitate, tum iucunditate ac dignitate. Sed de reliquis concisius, de præcipuis utilitatibus paulò largius dicam.
units.tr: Although many different subjects for an opening address present themselves, I feel that I am not now free to choose whatever I like, but must take up the subject I long ago undertook. For I think most of you, listeners, remember that last year, at about this same time, when I began to lecture on Ethical and Political Philosophy, after I had spoken of its origin and progress, and of its authors and cultivators, I promised that, as soon as an opportunity was given, I would speak from this place on the true praises of these disciplines and especially their uses. Indeed, I think no subject can now be devised that is better suited to stirring the minds of free and well-born men towards the studies of virtue and honour, of law and letters; or one more fitting to this our institution, this time, this place and this act, where rewards are given to virtue, learning and modesty; or, finally, one more pleasing to hear. I shall therefore speak, with the Lord Jehovah's help and, taking the time available into account, I shall speak briefly, on the chief fruit and praises of Political Philosophy: which consist, namely, in its remarkable usefulness and necessity, and in its pleasantness and dignity. But I shall deal with the remaining points more concisely, and with the chief uses somewhat more fully.

units.la: Quod dum peragere instituam: vos universos ac singu-los, los; Auditores; quanta possum obseruantia & diligentia, demisse & enixe oro, ut me solita vestra benignitate excipere, ac breuiter & tenuiter de proposito argumento perorantem beneuolo & æquo animo attendere non dedignemini. Dabitur à nobis opera, ut totus hic actus quàm fieri potest, expeditissimè ac planissimè percelebretur.
units.tr: As I set about doing this, I beg you all and each, listeners, with all the respect and diligence I can, humbly and earnestly, that you receive me with your customary kindness, and do not disdain to attend, with a benevolent and fair mind, to me as I speak briefly and modestly on the subject proposed. I will take care that this whole act is carried out as quickly and clearly as possible.

units.la: Politica igitur; si speciatim eam accipias; ad familiam Philosophiæ Practicæ spectat: sin autem generatim (vt nos hoc loco cum veteribus, cum Platone, & vspiam cum Aristotele) sumas: Nihil aliud est quàm ipsa Philosophia Practica: nimirum τῇ θεωρητικῇ[?], Contemplatiuæ (quam vocant) Philosophiæ opposita. Sed ne longius excurrat oratio, ad rem ipsam confestim accedemus: & eximiam Philosophiæ Politicæ dignitatem ac iucunditatem, itemque necessitatem, sed imprimis vtilitatem, principio generatim ex definitione, obiecto, & fine, deinde speciatim ex diuisione, eiusque membris, ostendemus.
units.tr: Political philosophy, then, if you take it in a specific sense, belongs to the family of Practical Philosophy; but if you take it in a general sense (as we do here with the ancients, with Plato, and with Aristotle wherever he is cited), it is nothing other than Practical Philosophy itself, set over against what is called contemplative philosophy [θεωρητικῇ]. But lest my speech run on too long, I shall come straight to the matter itself, and I shall show the outstanding dignity, pleasantness and necessity, but above all the usefulness, of Political Philosophy: first in general, from its definition, object and end, and then in particular, from its division and parts.

units.la: Cum igitur omnis quæ ratione suscipitur de re aliqua institutio, à definitione proficisci debeat; velut scitè & elegantèr M. Cicero in vestibulo primi Officiorum attestatur; vt nimirum rectius intelligatur, quid sit id de quo disputetur; eam ob rem mihi quoque exinde iam esse capienda dicendi primordia, facilè præsentisco. Est ergo Philosophia practica, generatim accepta & definita; doctrina quæ politicam hominum felicitatem, Legi naturæ congruenter agendo & viuendo, prudentiâ duce consequi docet: hoc est, doctrina de hominum studiis, moribus, & actionibus sic conformandis, vt conscientiæ seu naturæ legi, ac rectæ rationi consentiant, & ad practicam præsentis huius vitæ beatitudinem seu prosperitatem (quantam Dei benignitate consequi licet) per varia omnis generis (sed præsertim animi) ad eandem illam destinata bona, obtinendam conducant. Philosophia namque politica seu practica, omnia illa bonorum genera commonstrat ac pertractat, quæcunque præsentem hanc vitam, pro huius mundi captu, beant (bonum enim est quod beat) beant, inquam, hoc est, iuuant, sustentant, & exornant, hominemque mundano quodam modo perficiūt ac beatum reddunt; adeoque ad summum huius mundi (pro huius quidem seculi captu) bonum perducunt. Common-strat, inquam, & pertractat omnia illa bonorum genera, quibuscunque ad hanc vitam non tantum viuendam, sed commodè etiam & tranquillè, piè & honestè (hoc enim est feliciter) viuendam homo politicus opus habet: qualia sunt non externa duntaxat, sed etiam interna bona vitæque subsidia: quippe non fortunæ duntaxat & opes, sed disciplinæ quoque & artes: Eæque tum mechanicæ, tum Philosophicæ: sed leges quoque & sanctiones, eæque tum Oeconomicæ tum Politicæ; sed imprimis quoque virtutes, eæque tum Dianoëticæ, tum Ethicæ. Itaque Philosophia & beatitudo politica in cunctis ad hanc mundanam vitam honestè & commodè prosperéque traducēdam necessariis præsidiis: id est, in omnibus politicis, tũ internis, tũ externis, tum publicis, tum priuatis, tum animi, tum corporis, tum vitæ etiam seu fortunæ, bonis, tam adipiscendis & acquirendis, quàm conseruandis & augendis posita & occupata est. Rectè namque Plato. 7. de Repub. & 7. de Legibus, & Aristoteles Politicorum 8. primam ac potissimam in Republ. curam esse debere, aiunt; ut liberi ad omnia bonorum genera cognoscenda & quærenda erudiantur: imprimis autem cum artibus tum virtutibus instruantur. Ac scitè idem Plato alibi: Non minus ad Rempub. & omnium felicitatem interesse, ait, artes in politia bene constitui, quàm leges.
units.tr: Since every inquiry undertaken with reason about any matter ought to begin from a definition, as M. Cicero wisely and elegantly testifies at the beginning of the first book of On Duties, so that what is to be discussed may be better understood, I readily foresee that I too must begin my discourse from this point. Practical Philosophy, then, taken and defined in general, is the doctrine that teaches how to attain human political happiness by acting and living in accordance with the law of nature, under the guidance of prudence. That is, it is the doctrine of how human pursuits, morals and actions are to be shaped so that they agree with conscience or the law of nature and with right reason, and so that they help to obtain the practical happiness or prosperity of this present life (as far as God's goodness allows us to attain it), through various goods of every kind, but chiefly those of the mind, which are destined for that same end. For political or practical philosophy sets out and treats all those kinds of goods, whatever make this present life happy according to the measure of this world (for that is good which makes happy), make happy, I say, that is, help, sustain and adorn, and make a man in a worldly way complete and blessed; and so bring him to the highest good of this world (as far as this age can grasp it). It sets out and treats, I say, all those kinds of goods which a political man needs, not only in order to live this life but to live it conveniently and quietly, piously and honourably (for this is what it is to live happily). These are not only external goods and the supports of life, such as wealth and resources, but also skills and arts, both mechanical and philosophical; and laws and sanctions, both household and civil; and above all the virtues, both intellectual and ethical. Thus philosophy and political blessedness are concerned with, and occupied by, all the necessary supports for conducting this worldly life honourably, conveniently and prosperously: that is, with all political goods, both internal and external, public and private, of mind and body, and of life or fortune, both in obtaining and acquiring them and in preserving and increasing them. For Plato rightly says in the seventh book of the Republic and the seventh of the Laws, and Aristotle in the eighth book of the Politics, that the first and chief care of the commonwealth must be that children be taught to know and seek all kinds of good, and above all be equipped with arts and virtues. And Plato elsewhere wisely says that the establishment of good arts in a state matters no less to the commonwealth and the happiness of all than good laws do.

units.la: Sed quanquam istis omnibus hæc vita indiget: Legibus tamen honestis præcipuè indiget: virtutibus ethicis & dianoëticis imprimis indiget: Sed vera, inquam, pietate Deique cultu ac religione, & Iehouæ ter Optimi Maximique benignitate ac benedictione; etiam ad hanc politicam tranquillitatem ac prosperitatem; omnium maximè indiget. Enimverò secundum hæc tria, reliqua bonorum genera vitæque præsidia, & singula & vniuersa, tũ in œconomia, tum in Politia, gubernari & administrari, quæri & augeri, procurari & conseruari, doceri denique & addisci debent. Itaque leges honestæ certa reliquorū norma & regula sunt: Legū autem norma virtus est; Prudētia præsertim rationis rectæ magistra, itemque iustitia: virtutum denique ac reliquorum simul omnium, certissima norma, minimeque fallax regula, sacrosanctus Ethicæ diuinæ decalogus, pietasque & veritas Christianæ religionis est. Etenim vt Philosophia Politica cæterarum: ita hæc sola; Christiana, inquam, veritas ac pietas sola, omnium disciplinarum & artium longissimè princeps, ac vere ἀρχιτεκτονι[?]-κωτάτη est. Resp. nanque Christiana & magistratus Christianus, singularis esse debet custos ac Patronus totius decalogi, imo verbi Dei & Euangelij totius, velut Deuteronomij 17. Psalmo 2. & Iesaiæ 49 scriptum legimus.
units.tr: But although this life needs all these things, it needs honest laws above all; it needs ethical and intellectual virtues especially; but, I say, it needs most of all true piety, the worship and religion of God, and the goodness and blessing of Jehovah, thrice best and greatest, even for this political tranquillity and prosperity. Indeed, according to these three things, all the remaining kinds of good and supports of life, both singly and together, both in household management and in the state, must be governed and administered, sought and increased, procured and preserved, and finally taught and learned. Thus honest laws are the sure norm and rule of the rest; but the norm of laws is virtue, especially prudence, the teacher of right reason, and likewise justice; and finally, the most certain norm and least deceptive rule of all the virtues and the rest together is the sacred decalogue of divine ethics, and the piety and truth of the Christian religion. For just as Political Philosophy is the prince of the other disciplines, so this alone, I say, the Christian truth and piety alone, is by far the foremost of all disciplines and arts, and truly the most architectonic [ἀρχιτεκτονικωτάτη]. For the Christian commonwealth and the Christian magistrate ought to be the singular guardian and patron of the whole decalogue, indeed of the whole Word of God and the whole Gospel, as we read written in Deuteronomy 17, Psalm 2 and Isaiah 49.

units.la: Sed hactenus definitio Philosophiæ Politicæ exposita sit: Ex qua & obiectum eiusdem & finis, & summa illa, de qua nos præcipuè dicturi sumus, vtilitas, cuiuis facilè patescit. Obiectum igitur eius, sunt hominum mores, studia & actiones; Adeoque homo ipse totus, & vita eius, vitaque felicitas tota, cunctaque ad eam pie & honestè, commodè ac prosperè traducendam, necessaria bona atque præsidia. Principiò igitur homines ipsos, variosque variorum hominum mores, studia & actiones distinguet, ac distinctè; secundum leges ac virtutes distinctas; explicabit & informabit politicus: Deinde varia ista hominibus, sive singulis, sive coniunctis & communione aliqua, seu oeconomica seu politica, consociatis; ad obtinendam istam vitæ prosperitatem necessaria; tum priuata tum publica, tum interna animi & corporis, tum externa vitæ seu fortunæ bona atque præsidia ista, consimiliter distinguet, ac distinctè secundum easdem illas virtutes Ethicas, & leges sanctionesque oeconomicas & politicas explicabit, ac methodicè conformabit. Sed de obiecto, eiusque rectè describendi & conformandi ratione satis.
units.tr: But let the definition of Political Philosophy stand as set out so far. From it, the object of this science, its end, and that chief usefulness which we are especially going to speak of, are easily apparent to anyone. Its object, therefore, is the morals, pursuits and actions of human beings; and so the whole man and his life, the whole happiness of that life, and all the goods and safeguards needed to lead it piously, honourably, conveniently and prosperously. First, then, the politician will distinguish and set out the human beings themselves and the varied morals, pursuits and actions of various people, and will do so distinctly, according to their distinct laws and virtues. Next, he will likewise distinguish these various things needed by people, whether taken singly or joined together in some association, economic or political, for obtaining this prosperity of life: both private and public goods and safeguards, both inward goods of mind and body and outward goods of life or fortune. He will explain them distinctly, according to those same ethical virtues and the economic and political laws and sanctions, and arrange them in an orderly method. But enough about the object and the right way of describing and arranging it.

units.la: Finis denique præcipuus, &, vt loquuntur, summus
units.tr: Finally, the chief end of this philosophy, as they say, the highest end,

units.la: Philosophiæ huius, est politica siue mundana huius vitæ tranquillitas & honestas: hoc est, quantam Dei benignitate consequi licet, prosperitas terrena atque felicitas. Intermedij vero ad superiorem illum consequendum destinati ac subordinati fines, sunt illa ipsa, quæ diximus, omnis generis bona; sed interna præsertim; animi comprimis, deinde & corporis, rectè valentis, bona: præcipuè virtutes, mox iura & leges, tum artes liberales, deinde corporis sanitas: denique opificia & artificia honesta: postremò inter externa quidem bona; ante omnia, honesta nominis ac famæ, cum virtute & illæsa conscientia consentiens, integritas. Enimvero hæc sex bonorum genera, post religionis pietatem, omnium præstantissima maximèque necessaria exi stunt. Quocirca qui plura ex istis & insignio- ra sibi piè parauerit ac possederit: is iure optimo ditior aliis ac fortunatior, aut certè felicior ac beatior extiterit.
units.tr: is the political or worldly tranquillity and honesty of this life: that is, earthly prosperity and happiness, as far as it can be attained by the goodness of God. The intermediate ends, aimed at and subordinated to reaching that higher end, are the very goods we have mentioned, of every kind; but chiefly the inward ones: first those of the mind, above all, then those of the body when it is in good health: above all the virtues, then rights and laws, then the liberal arts, then health of body; finally, honest crafts and trades. Lastly, among the outward goods, before all else, the integrity of an honest name and reputation, agreeing with virtue and with an unharmed conscience. Indeed these six kinds of goods, after the piety of religion, are held to be the most excellent and most necessary of all. Wherefore whoever has piously acquired and possessed more of these, and more outstanding ones, has rightly become richer and more fortunate than others, or at least happier and more blessed.

units.la: Etenim hæc præ aliis diuina sunt, reliqua verò terrena: hæc sempiterna sunt, reliqua verò caduca: hæc firma & stabilia, reliqua verò fluxa & putrida: Hæc interna magis ac substantialia, aut iis certè proxima: reliqua vero externa & accidentaria: hæc animi, aut corporis ipsius propria; reliqua verò ab vtroque seiuncta: hæc hominem verè liberalem verèque bonum ac felicem reddunt: Reliqua verò sine istis, omnino illiberalem, sordidum, & infelicem efficiunt.
units.tr: For these goods are divine, beyond others, while the rest are earthly; these are everlasting, the rest perishable; these are firm and stable, the rest fluid and rotten. These are more inward and substantial, or at least very close to such; the rest are outward and accidental. These belong to the mind or the body itself; the rest are separated from both. These make a man truly free, truly good and happy; the rest, without these, make him wholly unfree, base and unhappy.

units.la: Verùm de definitione, deque obiecto ac fine Politicæ Philosophiæ satis: Nunc de partitione eius (vt distinctius omnia deinceps percipiantur) paucis dispiciamus. Politica ergo homine secularibus siue politicis honestè ac prosperè viuendi præceptis instruit; & ex variis istis bonorum generibus Politicam hominis, vitæque humanæ perfectionem ac felicitatem, in hoc æuo, quærit. Cùm verò homines aut singuli, ac per se spectentur, aut coniuncti, & cum aliis collati, aut utrique: hinc politica vitam & mores instruit, perfectionemque ac felicitatem quærit, hominum scilicet aut singulorum, aut coniunctorum, aut utrorumque, & omnium indistinctè. Coniunctorum, inquam, in sociesocietate vel domestica vel civili. Singulorum vitam & mores virtutibus instruit, perfectionemque ac felicitatem quaerit Ethica specialis. In societate domestica coniunctorum, œconomica: in civili sive urbana, politica, speciatim sic dicta. Utrorumque & omnium indistincte, Ethica seu politica generalis. Quanquam nihil opus erat vel Ethicam vel Politicam in generalem ac specialem (sicut vulgo tamen fit) distinguere. Quae enim omnium est & universorum indistincte, haec etiam singulorum est. Et quae non magis singulorum est, quam omnium, haec universorum est indistincte: quae non magis singulatim unumquenque, tanquam bonum virum, quam coniunctim bonum domesticum & patrem familias, aut bonum civem decet; haec non magis singulorum est, quam omnium & universorum, ac proinde utrorumque. Atenim Prudentia, fortitudo, temperantia, liberalitas, ac caeterae, non tam singulos decent, perficiunt ac beant, quam in œconomia & politica coniunctos, aut universos. Denique nec Aristoteles quadruplicem nobis Philosophię[?] practicæ disciplinam descripsit: Sed triplicem, Ethicen nimirum, œconomicen ac Politicen.
units.tr: But enough on the definition, the object and the end of Political Philosophy. Now let us briefly consider its division, so that everything may afterwards be grasped more distinctly. Political philosophy, then, instructs a man in the precepts of living honourably and prosperously in secular or civic matters, and from these various kinds of goods it seeks the political perfection and happiness of human life in this age. Since human beings are viewed either singly and in themselves, or joined together and compared with others, or both, politics instructs life and morals and seeks the perfection and happiness of people, that is, of individuals, of those joined together, or of both, and of all without distinction. Of those joined together, I say, in a society either domestic or civil. Ethics in particular instructs the life and morals of individuals by virtues and seeks their perfection and happiness. Economics concerns those joined in domestic society; politics, so called in particular, concerns civil or urban society. Ethics in general, or political science in general, concerns both and all without distinction. Yet there was no need to divide Ethics or Politics into general and special, as is nevertheless commonly done. For what belongs to all and to everyone without distinction, belongs also to individuals. And what belongs no more to individuals than to all, belongs to everyone without distinction: what befits each person singly, as a good man, no more than it befits jointly a good householder and father of a family, or a good citizen, belongs no more to individuals than to all and everyone, and therefore to both. For prudence, fortitude, temperance, liberality and the rest do not so much adorn, perfect and bless individuals as those joined together, or all, in economy and politics. Finally, Aristotle did not describe for us a fourfold discipline of practical philosophy, but a threefold one: namely Ethics, Economics and Politics.

units.la: Hæ tres disciplinæ omnes ac singulæ spectantur in imperio simul & obedientia. Ethica animam rationalem corpori, rectam rationem voluntati & appetitui imperare docet: Contra vero corpus animæ rationali, voluntatem & appetitum rectæ rationi obtemperare. Oeconomice domum & familiam totam prudenter administrare docet: Contra vero domesticos & familiares omnes oeconomo seu patrifamilias gnauiter obsecundare. Politice denique totum imperij ac politiæ, totum singulorum & coniunctorum, totum complurium collegiorum, familiarum ac subditorum corpus, iuste ac prudenter curare & gubernare docet: Contra vero omnes ac singulos, sive Collegij, sive familiæ, sive civitatis, socios ac subditos, legibus & magistratibus sedulo auscultare.
units.tr: All three of these disciplines, both together and each one, are considered in command and obedience. Ethics teaches that the rational soul should rule the body, and right reason should rule the will and appetite; conversely, that the body should obey the rational soul, and the will and appetite should obey right reason. Economics teaches how to administer the whole household and family prudently; conversely, that all domestic and household members should diligently obey the steward or head of the family. Politics, finally, teaches how to care for and govern justly and prudently the whole of the commonwealth and state, the whole of individuals and of those joined together, the whole body of many colleges, families and subjects; conversely, that all and each of the associates and subjects, whether of a college, a family or a city, should attentively obey the laws and magistrates.

units.la: Ethica sibiimperare, seque ipsum vincere docet: Oeconomica familiæ, Politica reipub. imperare docet: Ethica bonum virum, Oeconomica bonum familiæ patrem, & oeconomum, politica bonum ciuem & magistratum efficit, informat ac beat. Illa de virtutibus ac moribus præcipit: ista de domo & re familiari: Hæc de ciuitate & communi Reipub. salute: Illa singulorum, ista domesticorum, hæc ciuium ac populorum, beatitudinem seu prosperitatem procurat.
units.tr: Ethics teaches a man to rule himself and to conquer himself; Economics teaches to rule the family, Politics to rule the commonwealth. Ethics forms and makes blessed the good man, Economics the good father of the family and steward, Politics the good citizen and magistrate. The first gives precepts about virtues and morals; the second about the house and household property; the third about the state and the common welfare of the commonwealth. The first secures the blessedness or prosperity of individuals, the second of household members, the third of citizens and peoples.

units.la: Videtis, auditores, augustam Politicæ Philosophiæ ma-jestatem? cognoscitis summam eius dignitatem, & iucunditatem? perspicitis eximiam eius utilitatem?
units.tr: Do you see, hearers, the majesty of Political Philosophy? Do you recognise its supreme dignity and pleasantness? Do you perceive its outstanding usefulness?

units.la: Sed cùm Ethicam singulorum vitam & mores, instruere, perfectionemque ac beatitudinē quærere & procurare di-cimus: singulos illos intelligimus, in cœtu tamen aliquo ac societate politica degentes, siue unâ eademque, siue etiam diuersa; non autem solitarios plane, & ab aliis hominibus omninò ac perpetuò seiunctos: quibus nonnulli Ethicam specialem præscriptam & assignatam esse, perperam sanè (meo quidem iudicio) existimant.
units.tr: But when we say that Ethics instructs the life and morals of individuals, and seeks and secures their perfection and blessedness, we understand those individuals as living nonetheless in some company and political society, whether one and the same or also different, and not as wholly solitary and entirely and perpetually separated from other people. Some people, in my judgement certainly wrongly, think that a special Ethics is prescribed and assigned to such solitary persons.

units.la: Principiò namque Dei creatoris ordinatio obstat: deinde naturæ inclinatio: postea ipsius mundi constitutio: denique virtutum Ethicarum natura & affectio: quin & hominum inter homines ratio, sustentatio ac beatitudo. Etenim Deus creator hominem cum homine etiam ante natiuitatem statim in vtero coniungit ac deuincit: post natiuitatem verò matris gremio atque mammillis adhærescere voluit: quin & hominem ab homine educari & informari præcepit: hominem educatum homini, secundum Deum, & Ecclesiæ Dei, ac proximo, omnibus modis inseruire ac benefacere iusit. Ecquid enim secunda sacro-sancti decalogi tabula? nonne ardentissimum erga proximum amorem, beneuolentiam ac beneficentiam requirit? Nonne eandem tota & veteris & noui Testamenti scriptura requirit? Nonne eandem & charitas Christiana requirit? Quin & ipsa natura, Dei creatoris ministra, requirit. Quid enim storgæ naturales? an hominem ab homine dissodissociant aut disiungunt? Imò quid vniuersalis illa Naturæ ἔγκλισις? Nonne verisimè in Politicis ac Ethicis suis Aristoteles? Homo natura sua (ait primo politicorum secundo capite) societatis & congregationis humanæ studiosus est: Et quidem multo magis, quam vlla apis, aut vllum aliud animal ἀγελαῖον, quantumuis licet congregationis amantissimum. Quod & Cicero li. 2. de finibus innuit: cum formicas, apes, columbas, grues, hominum ac ciuitatis quodammodo cœtum imitari diserit. Quin & vocem ac sermonem (ait ibidem Aristoteles) Politicæ communionis & communicationis gratia homini natura concesit: priuatam vitam, priuatam prudentiam & vtilitatem, priuata cómoda atque negotia, ab œconomicis ac politicis separari, & sine ijsdem subsistere non posse idem eleganter lib.6. Ethicorum Nicomachicorum capite octauo ostendit. Sedenim & mundi ipsius constitutio talis est, prout nunc distributa sunt per terram imperia, vt, quocunque excurras, in ditionem ac territorium, adeoque in politiam aliquam incurras: Saltem in vniuersalem mundi politiam, cuius Monarcha Deus Iehoua est: qui vel naturæ ipsius, vel augustissimis sacrosancti decalogi legibus, te irretitum atque constrictum tenet: qui resonantissimo Euangelij sui clangore, ad Ecclesiam suam, ad conciones, ad preces, ad Sacramentorum administrationes publicè vnà cum alijs peragendas, ad charitatem Christiana erga alios exercendam, serio te reuocat. Quin & virtutum Ethicarum natura & affectio maximam sui partem talis est, vt eas sine altero, aut alteris, habere atque exercere non possis. Erga quem enim liberalis aut beneficus eris, si solitarius in eremo degas? Erga quem iustus? Erga quem mansuetus? contra quem fortis aut magnanimus? cui amicus? apud quos modestus vel vrbanus? Erga quos gratus? quibus clemens aut iratus?
units.tr: For first, the ordinance of God the Creator stands in the way; then the inclination of nature; next the constitution of the world itself; finally the nature and disposition of the ethical virtues; and indeed the relation, support and blessedness of human beings among human beings. For God the Creator joins and binds a human being to a human being even before birth, straightaway in the womb; and after birth he willed that the child should cling to the mother's lap and breasts; indeed he commanded that a human being be reared and formed by a human being, and, once reared, to serve and do good to another human being in every way, according to God, to the Church of God, and to one's neighbour. For what does the second table of the most sacred decalogue enjoin? Does it not require the most ardent love, goodwill and beneficence towards one's neighbour? Does not the whole of Scripture, both Old and New Testament, require the same? Does not Christian charity require the same? Indeed nature itself, the minister of God the Creator, requires it. For what are natural affections? Do they not join human beings to one another rather than separate or divide them? Indeed, what of that universal inclination of nature? Did not Aristotle truly say in his Politics and Ethics: man by nature (says the second chapter of the first book of the Politics) is inclined to society and human association? And indeed much more so than any bee or any other gregarious animal, however much it loves company. Cicero also hints at this in the second book of On Ends, when he says that ants, bees, doves and cranes somehow imitate the assembly of men and the state. Moreover, Aristotle says in the same place that nature gave man speech and discourse for the sake of political fellowship and communication; and the same author shows elegantly in the eighth chapter of the sixth book of the Nicomachean Ethics that private life, private prudence and advantage, and private conveniences and affairs, cannot be separated from economic and political matters and cannot subsist without them. But moreover the very constitution of the world is such, now that empires are distributed over the earth, that wherever you go you enter some dominion and territory, and so fall under some polity: at least under the universal polity of the world, whose Monarch is God Jehovah, who holds you entangled and bound either by nature itself or by the most august laws of the most sacred decalogue; who, with the resounding clangour of his Gospel, seriously calls you back to his Church, to sermons, to prayers, and to the public administration of the sacraments, to be performed together with others, and to the exercise of Christian charity towards others. Indeed, the nature and disposition of the ethical virtues is for the most part such that you cannot have or exercise them without another, or others. For to whom will you be liberal or beneficent if you live alone in the wilderness? Towards whom just? Towards whom gentle? Against whom brave or magnanimous? To whom a friend? Among whom modest or courteous? Towards whom grateful? To whom merciful or angry?

units.la: Itaque homo solitarius, non modò Politicus aut Oeconomicus esse non potest: Sed ne Ethicus quidem: quandoquidem virtutes pleraeque, non in habente aut possidente remanentac exercentut, sed ad alteros vnà viuen-tes referuntur,& ita demum consummantur. Denique & hominum inter homines ratio talis est, vt extra societa-tem, & in vita solitaria, nec sustentare fe, nec vlla beati-tudine practica frui posint: si quidem vni non suppetit ista bonorum variorum αὐτάρκεια, quæ ad huius vitæ su-stentationem desideratur: multò minùs quæ ad perse-ctionem aut beatitudinem vitæ huius politicam exopta-tur. Homo enim non tam propter se, quàm propter Ec-clesiam, & proximum, à Deo conditus est: Homo homi-nis causa creatus. Perelegantèr igitur ex Platone Tullius primo Officiorum: Non nobis solum nati sumus, sed or-tus nostri partem sibi patria vendicat, partem parentes, partem amici. Vnde si quis solitarius eremita planè se ab hominibus segreget: Is Timon μισάνθρωπος erit, patriam, rempub., parentes, amicos, quibus se totum debet, frau-dabit: eosque homine ac ciue, ab ipsis nato & educato, vestito & enutrito dispoliabit. Quapropter ex his omnibus liquidò consequitur: Nullam esse solitariis aut eremi-tis præscriptam Ethicen: Adeoque singulos, quos Ethi-ca informare dicitur, intelligendos esse, in cœtu tamen aliquo ac societate vel Oeconomica, vel Politica, vel vtraque degentes: quandoquidem extra societatem & in vita planè solitaria, nemo hominum commodè viuere, seque sustentare, vel vlla beatitudine practica frui po-teft.
units.tr: Therefore a solitary man cannot be a political or domestic man, and not even an ethical one, since most virtues do not remain in the person who has or possesses them but are exercised and directed toward others living alongside him, and only so are they brought to completion. Indeed, human beings stand in such a relation to one another that outside society, in a solitary life, they can neither sustain themselves nor enjoy any practical blessedness. A single man does not have that self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκεια] of various goods which is needed to sustain this life, much less that which is desired for the perfection and political happiness of this life. For man was created by God not so much for his own sake as for the Church and his neighbour: man was created for the sake of man. So Tully, following Plato, says very elegantly in the first book of De Officiis: "We are not born for ourselves alone; our country claims a part of our birth, our parents a part, our friends a part." Hence, if anyone as a solitary hermit completely withdraws from men, he will be a Timon, a hater of mankind. He will defraud his country, the commonwealth, his parents and friends, to whom he owes himself entirely, and he will strip of their character as men and citizens those from whom he was born and educated, clothed and nourished. From all this it clearly follows that there is no ethics prescribed for solitaries or hermits. The individuals whom ethics is said to form must therefore be understood as living in some assembly and society, whether domestic or political or both, since outside society and in a wholly solitary life no one can live decently, support himself, or enjoy any practical blessedness.

units.la: Sed de hac quæstione nil attinet plura dicere. Itaque in viam redeamus: & ad thema nobis propositum; de quo hactenus paulò generalius disseruimus; deinceps propius accedamus, ac de Philosophiæ Politicæ seu prac-ticæ vtilitatibus paulò presfius ac penitius disseramus: quæ sanè tot & tantæ sunt, vt qui eas omnes ac singulas dicendo percensere velit, Libyci velit æquoris idem Dicere quàm multa Zephyro turbentur arenæ
units.tr: But there is no point in saying more about this question. Let us return to our path and to the subject set before us, of which we have so far spoken in rather general terms. Let us now come closer to it and discuss more precisely and thoroughly the usefulness of political or practical philosophy. These uses are so many and so great that anyone who wished to list them all, one by one, would be like one who wishes to say how many grains of sand are stirred by the Zephyr on the Libyan sea.

units.la: Itaque præcipuas nunc delibasse satis fuerit. Cum ergò[?] multa sint in Philosophia & grauia & vtilia, accuratè copiosèque à Philosophis disputata (vt verissimè primo Officiorũ Tullius) latissimè tamen patere videntur ea, quæ de officijs tradita ab illis atque præcepta sunt: quæ inquâ, de virtutibus, moribus, & actionibus, quæque de tran-quillitate ac prosperitate hominum, vitæque & societatis humanę, tum œconomicæ, tum politicę, tradita sunt. Nul-la enim vitæ pars, neq; publicis, neq; priuatis neq; forensi-bus, neq; domesticis in rebus, neq; si tecũ ipse agas quid, neq; si cum altero contrahas, officio vacare, & isto, inquâ, Philosophiæ practicæ studio carere potest: in eoque ex-colendo sita vitæ est honestas omnis, atque in negligendo turpitudo. Et quis est, qui nullis officij virtutisque præce-ptis tradendis Philosophum se audeat dicere? Hæc Cice-ro. Quare cum Philosophia tota frugifera, & fructuosa sit (vt idem in vestibulo tertij Officiorum innuit) siue scilicet infera, siue supera, siue mundana, siue cœlestia, siue mate-rialia, siue à materia abstracta, perscrutetur: Nullus tamen in ea locus feracior aut vberior, nulla eius pars vtilior aut præstantior est, quam hæc de virtutibus & officijs, de vita & moribus, de felicitate & actionibus, tum singulorum, tum plurium, aut vniuersorum, disciplina. Hæc; quantum natura tum in singulis hominum actionibus, & vita tota, tum in œconomia, tum in politia, possit, ostendit. Hæc ve-rum bonorum & malorum, honestorum & turpium, vti-lium & inutiliũ, discrimen, prudentia duce, aperit: Omnis virtutis & honestatis politicæ, omniumque actionum & legum honestarum fontes inquirit & exponit. Hæc rectam rationem ad omnia ista instruit: Et honestè ac tranquillè, commodè ac prosperè, & viuendi, & vnà viuendi normam, omniumque honestarum actionum, morum, atque legum regulam tradit. Hæc de societatum, & communionum humanarum generibus, de imperiorum & magistratuum, judiciorum & senatuum, speciebus, formis, ac differentijs disserit. Hæc vitam hominis prius efferam & horridam, à barbarie ad lenitatem, ab immanitate ad humanitatem, ad rectæ ratiónis obsequium, ad communem ciuilitatē, & ciuilem communionem societatemque colendam traduxit. Et ita miseros mortales miserè alioqui dispersos ac dissipatos in domos & familias primùm, mox in vicos, deinde in vrbes, oppida & ciuitates, tandem in prouincias, regna & imperia collegit & compegit: Legesque, magistratus, & ordinem politicum instituit. Hæc generis humani, ea ipsa parte, qua maximè turpificatum, afflictum & vulneratū est, sola, post Deum ac Scripturam sacram, medicina & instauratio superest: licet paucissimi (proh pudor) huic sese medicinæ secundum virtutis præscriptum curandos præbeant: Sed multò plures apertum omni virtuti, & honestati veræ bellum indicant. Hæc plurima ac diuersissima omnis generis bona, ad vitæ honestatem ac prosperitatem necessaria: tum interna tum externa, tum publica, tum priuata, tum animi, tum corporis, bona, desiderat&commonstrat; quadamtenus etiam suppeditat & conseruat: atque ita hominum, tum singulorum, tum plurium & vniuersorum beatitudinem seu prosperitatē, tum Ethicam, tum Oeconomicam & Politicam procurat.
units.tr: So it will be enough to have touched on the chief ones. Since philosophy contains many weighty and useful matters, discussed carefully and at length by philosophers (as Tully says most truly in the first book of De Officiis), those things seem to reach most widely which have been handed down and prescribed about duties: that is, about virtues, morals and actions, and about the tranquillity and prosperity of men and of human life and society, both domestic and political. For no part of life, whether public or private, forensic or domestic, whether you are dealing with yourself or contracting with another, can be free of duty, nor can it lack this study of practical philosophy. In cultivating it lies all the honour of life, and in neglecting it all its baseness. And who would dare to call himself a philosopher without teaching the precepts of duty and virtue? So Cicero. Therefore, since the whole of philosophy is fruitful and productive (as the same author hints at the beginning of the third book of De Officiis), whether it investigates lower things or higher, worldly or heavenly, material or abstracted from matter, yet no place in it is richer or more fertile, and no part of it more useful or excellent, than this teaching on virtues and duties, on life and morals, on happiness and actions, whether of individuals, of many, or of all. This teaching shows how far nature can reach, both in the individual actions and whole life of men and in household management and government. With prudence as its guide, it reveals the distinction between true good and evil, the honourable and the shameful, the useful and the useless; it inquires into and sets out the sources of all political virtue and honour, of all actions and honourable laws. It instructs right reason in all these matters, and it hands down the rule of living honourably and quietly, usefully and prosperously, and of living together, and the standard of all honourable actions, morals and laws. It discourses on the kinds, forms and differences of human societies and communities, of empires and magistrates, of courts and senates. This teaching has led human life, once wild and rough, from barbarity to gentleness, from savagery to humanity, to obedience to right reason, and to the cultivation of common civility and civil fellowship and society. And so it gathered and bound together wretched mortals, who were otherwise wretchedly scattered and dispersed, first into households and families, then into villages, then into towns, cities and states, and finally into provinces, kingdoms and empires; and it established laws, magistrates and political order. In the very part of the human race where it has been most defiled, afflicted and wounded, this teaching alone, after God and Holy Scripture, remains as medicine and restoration; although very few (for shame!) allow themselves to be cured by this medicine according to the prescription of virtue, while far more openly declare war on all virtue and true honour. This teaching demands and shows the many and most diverse goods of every kind needed for the honour and prosperity of life, whether inner or outer, public or private, goods of the mind or of the body; to some extent it also supplies and preserves them. And so it promotes the happiness or prosperity of men, whether of individuals, of many, or of all, in ethics, economics and politics alike.

units.la: Quamobrem, Auditores, nulla fermè pars Philosophiæ, cognitione ac pertractatione jucundior & liberalior est, nulla fructu vtilitateque præstantior, nulla dignitate illustrior, nulla ad liberam animi recreationem, & ingenuo homine dignam oblectationem cōmodior: nulla denique rebus ac necessitatibus humanis conuenientior. Cæteræ profectò artes ac nunquā satis laudatæ disciplinæ philosophicæ, odoratissimas suas lauros & elegantissimas suas hederas habent, sed ad hanc, vt ad reginā, & architectatricem (teste philosopho) referuntur. Merito itaque M. Cicero secundo Officiorum exclamat, se non intelligere, ecquid tandem sit, quod ille laudandum putet, qui tantæ sapientiæ studium vituperat. Videtis, Auditores, augustam politicæ philosophiæ maiestatem? cognoscitis summam eius dignitatem & iucunditatem? perspicitis eximiam eius tum vtilitatem tum necessitatem.
units.tr: For this reason, gentlemen, almost no part of philosophy is more pleasant or more liberal to know and handle, none more excellent in fruit and usefulness, none more illustrious in dignity, none more suited to the free refreshment of the mind and to delight worthy of a free man, none finally more fitting to human affairs and needs. The other arts and philosophical disciplines, never praised enough, indeed have their most fragrant laurels and most elegant ivy; but they are referred to this one as to a queen and architect (as the philosopher witnesses). Rightly, therefore, Marcus Cicero exclaims in the second book of De Officiis that he does not understand what anyone could think worthy of praise who condemns the pursuit of so great wisdom. Do you see, gentlemen, the august majesty of political philosophy? Do you recognise its supreme dignity and pleasantness? Do you perceive its outstanding usefulness and necessity?

units.la: Neque tamen generalis ista; de qua modò diximus; Philosophia politica seu practica sola, tantopere iucunda & splendida, vtilis & necessaria est: Sed Ethica quoque & Oeconomica consimiles promerentur laudes. Ethica naturæ seu conscientiæ legem exponit: barbarorum & agrestium hominum conscientiam stertentem expergefacit, deque communibus honestatis sequendæ ac turpitudinis fugiendæ notitijs, ac Principijs practicis commonefacit, adeoque Deum mundi autorem & rerum omnium creatorem esse, itemque iustum ac seuerum flagitiorum vindicem, summè bonum, sapientem, veracem, omnique ex parte beatum esse; id, inquam, Ethica seu lex naturæ per Ethicam explicata conscientiam rectius erudit, atque conuincit: Ethnicos denique (de quo & Apostolus ad Romanos secundo capite) coram tribunali Dei inexcusabiles reddit. Ethica naturam, & vires hominis perspicere, seque ipsum nosse docet: quod summæ sapientiæ est, teste Socrate in dialogo Platonis, qui Amatorum aut Philosophiæ nomine inscribitur. Hæc vna Philosophia (ait M. Tullius lib. 1. de Legibus) id quod difficilimum est, docuit: Nempe vt nosmetipsos nosceremus. Ex qua videlicet notitia, homo virtutem & honestatem suæ naturæ, dignitati ac præstantiæ imprimis conuenire, turpitudinem autem & vitia eidem maximè repugnare cognoscit. Et quoniam post miserabilem illam primorum parentum ruinâ, ita, proh dolor, comparatum est, vt inferior hominis pars imperium sibi deposcat, & corpus animæ; affectus, libidines, & appetitus, rationi præscribere ac dominari contendat; Ethica rationi suppetias gnauiter ferre laborat, & quò nos recta ratio vocet, & cur ei, tanquam dominæ, obtemperandum sit, declarat. Neque rationi tantùm, sed & voluntati per virtutem suppetias ferre desiderat. Affectibus vitiosis nil immanius, virtute nil humanius: libidinibus nil impurius, virtute nil sanctius: appetitionib. prauis nil tetrius, virtute nil amabilius: voluptate nil insidiosius, virtute nil candidius. Verumenimverò Ethica turbulen-tis istis ac seditiosis in hominis Microcosmo, in hominis, inquam sinu & gremio, numero maximo delitescenti-bus ac turmatim congregatis civibus; quin potius tyran-nis aut hostibus, voluptatibus, dico, libidinibus, affecti-bus, & appetitionibus prauis, rationis rectæ ac virtutis adminiculo strenuè resistit. Voluptas (ut eximiè dixit exi-mius Plato) est esca malorum, qua homines capiuntur, nō secus atque hamo pisces. Voluptas est blandissima domi-na, boni quidem imitatrix, sed reuera honestati, virtuti & rationi inimica, malorum omnium mater, & illecebra turpitudinis, ut politissimè dixit politissimus Cicero in libro de Legib. in officijs, ac de finibus. Verumenimverò hanc detegit & in lucem protrahit virtus: Hanc compescit aut corrigit virtus: hanc sibi subiicit, aut expellit virtus. His omnibus, Auditores, quid utilius humano ge-neri nō iam dici, sed vel excogitari potest? quid robustius? quid firmius? quid salubrius? quid preciosius.
units.tr: Yet it is not political or practical philosophy alone, in this general sense of which we have just spoken, that is so very pleasant and splendid, useful and necessary. Ethics and economics likewise deserve similar praise. Ethics sets out the law of nature or of conscience. It awakens the snoring conscience of barbarians and rustic people, and reminds them of the common notions of following honour and avoiding shame, and of practical principles; and so it teaches and more surely convinces the conscience that God is the author of the world and the creator of all things, and likewise the just and severe avenger of crimes, supremely good, wise, truthful, and in every respect blessed. Ethics, or the law of nature as explained through ethics, I say, instructs and convicts the conscience more rightly, and finally renders the heathen (as the Apostle also says in Romans, chapter 2) inexcusable before the tribunal of God. Ethics teaches man to perceive the nature and powers of man and to know himself; which, as Socrates teaches in Plato's dialogue entitled Lovers or Philosophy, is the height of wisdom. This one philosophy, says Marcus Tullius in the first book of On Laws, has taught what is most difficult: namely, that we should know ourselves. From this knowledge, certainly, man learns that virtue and honour are especially fitting to the dignity and excellence of his nature, while shame and vices are very much opposed to it. And since, after that miserable ruin of our first parents, it has come about, alas, that the lower part of man demands rule for itself, and the body seeks to prescribe to and dominate the soul, its affections, lusts and appetites, ethics labours vigorously to bring aid to reason, and it declares whither right reason calls us and why we must obey it as our mistress. And it seeks to bring aid through virtue not only to reason but also to the will. Nothing is more savage than vicious affections, nothing more humane than virtue; nothing more impure than lusts, nothing more holy than virtue; nothing more foul than wicked appetites, nothing more lovable than virtue; nothing more treacherous than pleasure, nothing more sincere than virtue. Indeed, ethics strenuously resists those turbulent and seditious citizens who hide in vast numbers in the microcosm of man, in the very bosom and lap of man, and gather together in crowds; or rather, the tyrants and enemies, I mean pleasures, lusts, affections and wicked appetites, it resists with the help of right reason and virtue. Pleasure (as the most excellent Plato said most excellently) is the bait of evils, by which men are caught just as fish are caught by a hook. Pleasure is a most flattering mistress, an imitator of good but in truth hostile to honour, virtue and reason, the mother of all evils and the allurement of baseness, as the most refined Cicero said most refinedly in his books On Laws, On Duties and On Ends. Yet virtue uncovers pleasure and drags it into the light; virtue restrains or corrects it; virtue subjects it to itself or drives it out. Gentlemen, what more useful thing for the human race can now be said, or even imagined, than all this? What more robust? What more firm? What more wholesome? What more precious?

units.la: Quanquam igitur & plurimas & eximias laudes jure optimo promeretur Ethica: tamen vel hoc uno nomine omnibus quàm commendatissima esse debet: quòd varias omnis generis ac diuersissimas virtutes profitetur. Virtus autem per se ipsa laudabilis est: & sine ea nil potest laudari, ut verissimè Cicero de Oratore. Enimverò virtute nil formosius, nil pulchrius, nil laudabilius, nil amabilius, nil homine dignius: quippe quæ in tenebris lucet, ac per se semper splendet, nec alienis unquam sordibus obsolescit, ut idem eleganter pro Sestio. Is ergo gloria maximè excellit, qui virtute plurimum præstat; quippe gloria virtutem tanquam umbra solem, aut corpus soli obiectum comitatur: Et justa gloria est fructus veræ virtutis honestissimus, ut idem in Tusculanis, pro Planco & in Pisonem. Virtus denique & sola, & semper libera est, quæ, etiamsi corpora capta sint armis, & constricta vincu-lis, tamen ius suum, & omnium rerum impunitam libertaem tenet; vt idem Cicero de Oratore ait. Ad summam: virtus vna omnium, omnibus antecellit maximè. Vin' tibi preciosissimas gemmas comparare? virtutes Ethicas; cū Christiana tamē pietate coniunctas; tibi comparato. Vin' Carbunculum ignis instar fulgentissimum? En tibi sapientiam aut prudentiā in mente coruscantem. Vin' tibi Chrysolithum, aut Carchedonium, Stellæ instar lucentem? En tibi auream illam Iustitiam. Vin' Adamantem infrācū? En tibi infractam animi fortitudinem. Vin' Sapphirum aut Smaragdum occulta venena & scorpionum ictus sanante? En tibi temperantiam, aut continentiam, occulta & fraudulenta blandissimæ illius dominæ, voluptatis, ac libidinis, venena curantem. Quot igitur virtutes tibi suppeditat Ethica, tot gemmas preciosissimas tibi suppeditat. Quinimò virtus quouis nobilissimo auro, quauis splendidissima & preciosissima gemma, nobilior, splendidior ac preciosior est. Gemmæ corporis bona sunt, virtutes animi. Corpus terrenum est, animus cœlestis ac diuinus. Corpus mortale, animus immortalis. Vt ergo stellæ in cœlo lucent: sic virtutes in animo. Sapientia & prudentia sunt instar solis inter virtutes dianoëticas: Iustitia verò instar solis inter virtutes Ethicas seu practicas. Quinimò sol interdiu duntaxat mundum illustrat; Sapientia, prudentia, & iustitia, etiam noctu, & quouis tempore coruscant, hominemque & politicam hominum societatem conseruant. Rectissimè igitur quinto Ethicorum Philosophus: Neque Lucifer, neque Hesperus, ita pulcher aut clarus ac serenus est, vt iustitia. Quamobrem Ethica de virtutibus tractans Philosophia ad varias, easque arduas sæpe & spinosas, in omni hominum vita & negotiis, in commerciis, in consiliis, in iudiciis, quæstiones, non vtilis tantùm, sed necessaria plane est.
units.tr: Although Ethics rightly earns many outstanding praises, it ought to be most commended to everyone for this one reason alone: it teaches every kind of virtue, all of them varied and very different from one another. Virtue is praiseworthy in itself, and nothing can be praised without it, as Cicero says very truly in De Oratore. Indeed, nothing is more graceful, more beautiful, more praiseworthy, more lovable, or more worthy of a human being than virtue. It shines in the dark and always glows by its own light, and it never grows dull through any foreign filth, as the same author says elegantly in the Pro Sestio. So the one who excels most in glory is the one who surpasses others most in virtue, for glory follows virtue as a shadow follows a body or as a body stands in the sun. True glory is the most honourable fruit of genuine virtue, as the same author says in the Tusculan Disputations, in the Pro Plancio, and in the In Pisonem. Finally, virtue alone is always free. Even if the body is seized by arms and bound in chains, virtue keeps its own right and an unassailable freedom over all things, as the same Cicero says in De Oratore. In short, virtue alone surpasses all things above all. Do you want to acquire the most precious gems? Acquire the ethical virtues, joined with Christian piety. Do you want a carbuncle, shining bright as fire? Here is wisdom or prudence, flashing in your mind. Do you want a chrysolite, or a carchedony, gleaming like a star? Here is that golden Justice. Do you want an unbreakable adamant? Here is an unbroken fortitude of soul. Do you want a sapphire or an emerald to heal hidden poisons and the stings of scorpions? Here is temperance, or self-restraint, which cures the hidden and deceitful poisons of that most seductive mistress, pleasure and lust. Therefore, as many virtues as Ethics supplies to you, so many most precious gems it supplies. Indeed, virtue is nobler, brighter and more precious than any most noble gold or any most splendid and precious gem. Gems are goods of the body; virtues are goods of the soul. The body is earthly, the soul heavenly and divine; the body is mortal, the soul immortal. As the stars shine in heaven, so do the virtues in the soul. Wisdom and prudence are like the sun among the intellectual virtues, while justice is like the sun among the ethical or practical virtues. Indeed, the sun lights the world only by day, but wisdom, prudence and justice shine at night too and at all times, and they preserve both the individual man and the political society of men. Therefore the philosopher rightly says in the fifth book of the Ethics: "Neither Lucifer nor Hesperus is so beautiful, or so bright and serene, as justice." Hence Philosophy, when it treats of the virtues in Ethics, is not merely useful but plainly necessary for the many questions, often difficult and thorny, that arise in all of human life and affairs: in dealings, in counsels, and in judgments.

units.la: M. Brutus, vnus ex iis qui Cæsarem Dictatorem confoderant, in campis Philippicis postea ab Octauio & Antonio victus, necem sibi conscGuit. M. Cato Vticensis, post Pharsalicam cladem reliquias Pompeiani exercitus colle-dit: Sed Scipione tandem à Cæsare victo, Vticæ, quam tu-tandam sumserat, necem sibi consciuit, perlecto prius Phædone, Platonis de animæ immortalitate dialogo. M. Antonius Triumuir, M. Oratoris filius, Antigonūludæo-rum regem secuti percusit, quod antea nulli regum isto-rum contigerat: congrediens postea cum Octauio Augu-sto, victus, Alexandriam confugiens, ibidem obsessus, gla-dio se interemit. Lucretia illa Romana, à Sexto Tarquinio vi stuprata, sempiternum dedecus metuens, pugiun-culo se necauit. Hæc, & alia iis similia, sunt etiam hodie fermè quotidiana. Isti putabant viri fortis esse, seipsum potius perdere, quàm hosti dedere. Hæc vero putabat fortis & castæ matronæ esse, sibi ipsi potius necem conscisce-re, quam diuturnam nominis & existimationis ignomi-niaferre. Speciosa plerisque ratio videtur. At Philosophia Ethica forinsecus speciosam quidem, reuera autem frigi-dam ac friuolam existimat. Quia se ipsum necare, viri ne-quaquam fortis est, sed desperantis, acproinde extremo metu & dolore laborantis. Metus enim est molesta, omnisq; doloris impatiens imminentis mali expectatio: Cu-ius comites & effecta sunt diffidentia ac desperatio. Vir autem fortis, quandiu fortis est, nunquam animum abii-cit, nunquam diffidit aut desperat. Isti ergo omnes & eorum similes, minime fortes, quia ne seipsos quidem vice-runt, nedum alios: sed à se ipsis & à suis affectibus ac mœroribus victi & mactati sunt. Deinde minime etiam fortes propterea; quia mortem sibi consciscere, est ipsam naturam confodere; quæ atrocissimum Phalaridis taurū omniaq; alia supplicia millies potius tolerare, quā se ipsum necare inbet. Se ipsum iugulare, est civitati, patriæ, cognatis, amicis, liberis, quib. omnes nati sumus, grande iniuriā facere; adeoque civem furari: Est leges violare, seque infamē reddere: Leges enim sempiternam nominis ignominiam talibus statuunt, adeoque terram & sepulturam eis non concedunt: Est diuinam maiestatem Dei, qui vitam dedit, ludificare, & ad celerem vindictam exuscitare: Est denique contra rectam rationem, & contra virtutem agere. Etenim virtus primò requirit, vt agens sciat & intelligat quid agat: deinde vt agat ex προαιρέσεως[?] id est vt bonū actionis finem & scopum, vt honestum ac prudenter deliberatum & praemeditatum propositum habeat: adeoque vt agat amore ipsius virtutis, & honestatis; non metus, non periculi, non doloris, non quaestus, aut alterius rei gratia, vel impulsu. Postea requirit virtus, vt agens bona & honesta media quaerat, quibus bonum illum finem consequi possit. Denique vt bona media legitimo ac honesto & liberali agendi modo, diligenter obseruatis ac diiudicatis omnibus circumstantiis circumspectè ac prudenter ad praxin accommodet. Itaque nec mors spontanea & vltro adscita, illos magnanimos effecit, nec pugiunculus Lucretiae, eam aut caltam aut fortem reddidit. Quae omnia, & cuncta similia, vnica post sacrosanctam Theologiam, Philosophia Ethica ostendit, & conuincit. Videtis igitur Auditores, augustam Ethicae Philosophiae maiestatem? cognoscitis summam eius dignitatem? perspicitis eximiam eius vtilitatem? Ethica est vitae & morum honestorum norma, virtutum magistra, actionum laudabilium regula. Haec morbos animi dispellere, affectus sedare, rationem prudenter regere, vitam totam virtutum quasi gemmis & ornamentis exornare docet. Vt medicina corporis mala: ita haec animi vitia sanat: Imò totius hominis vtilitatem ac felicitatem procurat. Polemo Atheniensis adolescentiam suam agebat in omnibus deliciis, ac voluptatibus: In lustris nanque, popinis, conuiuiis, omnibusque locis, ita verbis & factis, ita gestu & incessu se gerebat, vt non iam petulans duntaxat, verum perditus omnino ac desperatus videretur. Sed cum ebrius aliquando ac fertis redi-mitus, vna cum sociis ac ministris libidinum suarum, Scholam Xenocratis Philosophi Platonici ingressus esset, & huc de temperantiæ & continentiæ laudibus egregiè ac seue-rè perorantem audiuisset, sic repente affectus & mutatus est, vt mox ab istis adolescentiæ cupiditatibus ac libidini-bus abductus, & ad virtutis ac liberalium disciplinarum studium, traductus fuerit, magnusque tandem Philoso-phus euaserit.
units.tr: Marcus Brutus, one of those who stabbed the dictator Caesar, was afterwards defeated by Octavian and Antony on the plains of Philippi, and he killed himself. Marcus Cato of Utica, after the defeat at Pharsalus, gathered the remnants of Pompey's army. But when Scipio was finally defeated by Caesar, Cato killed himself at Utica, which he had taken up to defend, having first read the Phaedo, Plato's dialogue on the immortality of the soul. Marcus Antonius the triumvir, son of the orator Marcus, had Antigonus, king of the Jews, executed by the sword, which had happened to none of the kings before him. Later, when he came to grips with Octavian Augustus and was defeated, he fled to Alexandria, was besieged there, and ran himself through with his sword. That Roman Lucretia, violated by force by Sextus Tarquinius, fearing everlasting disgrace, killed herself with a small dagger. These deeds, and others like them, still happen almost daily. Those men thought it was the mark of a brave man to destroy himself rather than surrender to the enemy; and Lucretia thought it was the mark of a brave and chaste matron to take her own life rather than bear the lasting shame and disgrace of her name and reputation. To many people this reasoning seems plausible. But Ethical Philosophy judges it to be specious on the outside, yet in truth cold and frivolous. For to kill oneself is in no way the act of a brave man, but of a man in despair, and therefore of one suffering from extreme fear and pain. For fear, the expectation of an impending evil, is troubling and unable to endure any suffering, and its companions and results are distrust and despair. But a brave man, for as long as he is brave, never gives up his spirit, never distrusts or despairs. So all those men and their like were not brave at all, since they did not even conquer themselves, much less others; they were overcome and slaughtered by themselves and by their own passions and sorrows. Moreover, they were not brave for this further reason: to take one's own life is to stab nature herself, and nature bids us endure the most savage torture of Phalaris' bull, and all other punishments, a thousand times over rather than kill ourselves. To cut one's own throat is a great wrong against the state, the fatherland, kinsmen, friends and children, to whom we are all born; it is in effect to rob the citizen. It is to violate the laws and render oneself infamous, for the laws decree everlasting disgrace for such people and do not allow them burial in the ground. It is to mock the divine majesty of God, who gave life, and to provoke swift vengeance. And finally, it is to act against right reason and against virtue. For virtue first requires that the agent know and understand what he is doing; then that he act from a deliberate choice [προαιρέσεως], that is, that he have before him a good aim and goal of the action, a purpose that is honourable, prudently deliberated and premeditated; and so that he act out of love of virtue and honour itself, not out of fear, danger, pain, gain, or for some other reason or impulse. Next, virtue requires that the agent seek good and honest means by which he can reach that good end. Finally, that he apply the good means in practice in a lawful, honest and free manner, carefully observing and weighing all the circumstances, and acting cautiously and prudently. Thus neither a voluntary death, chosen of one's own accord, made those men great-souled, nor did Lucretia's small dagger make her either wise or brave. Ethical Philosophy, second only to sacred Theology, shows and proves all these things and everything like them. Do you see, listeners, the majestic dignity of Ethical Philosophy? Do you recognise its high worth? Do you perceive its outstanding usefulness? Ethics is the rule of life and of honourable conduct, the teacher of the virtues, the standard of praiseworthy actions. It teaches us to drive away diseases of the soul, to calm the passions, to govern reason prudently, and to adorn the whole of life as with gems and ornaments of virtue. As medicine cures the ills of the body, so this cures the vices of the soul; indeed it secures the usefulness and happiness of the whole man. Polemo of Athens spent his youth in every kind of delight and pleasure: in brothels, taverns, banquets and all places, he so conducted himself in word and deed, in gesture and bearing, that he seemed not merely wanton but utterly abandoned and past hope. But once, when he entered the school of Xenocrates, the Platonic philosopher, drunk and wreathed with garlands, together with his companions and the servants of his lusts, and heard him holding forth earnestly and severely on the praises of temperance and self-restraint, he was so suddenly moved and changed that, drawn away from the desires and lusts of his youth, he was led to the pursuit of virtue and the liberal disciplines, and at last became a great philosopher.

units.la: Sed longius exspaciatur oratio. Itaque de Ethica eiusq; præcipuis vtilitatibus satis: & de œconomica alio tempo-re: Nunc ad Politicam reuertamur: & iis quæ supra dixi-mus, paucula addamus. Hæc nil aliud est, quam totius Phi-losophiæ, & omnium aliarum disciplinarum & artium, ad politicam hominis salutem ac prosperitatem comparata praxis quædam. Itaque toti humano generi, singulis & vni-uersis, seorsim & coniunctim, seu priuatum, aut Oecono-micum, seu publicum, aut Politicum statum spectes, non modò vtilis, sed omnib. modis necessaria est: ad imperia, politias, respub., ad Ecclesias & scholas, tum constituen-das, tum conseruandas, accommodatissima. Hæc; Si præ-sertim cum sacrosancta Theologia, vti par est, sedulò con-iungatur; omnibus artibus ac disciplinis, omnibus opifi-ciis & artificiis honestis, scholis & Ecclesiis hospitium præ-bet, ac patrocinatur. Quàm igitur est vtile ac salutare ha-bere politias & respub., easque recta imperij formâ pru-denter constitutas; habere bonos Magistratus, curias & Senatus, iudicia, leges, habere Scholas & Ecclesias, omnis generis artes & disciplinas, tum Philosophicas tum me-chanicas; habere denique bonos ciues, artifices & opifi-ces: tam vtilis quoque & salutaris est Philosophia Practica seu Politica.
units.tr: But my speech wanders too far. So let that suffice concerning Ethics and its principal usefulness; and I shall speak of household economy at another time. Now let us return to Politics and add a few things to what I have said above. This is nothing other than a certain practice of all Philosophy and of all the other disciplines and arts, directed to the political welfare and prosperity of man. Therefore, whether you look at the whole human race, at individuals and at all people, separately and together, or at the private, household, or public and political condition, it is not only useful but necessary in every way, and most suited to establishing and preserving empires, polities, commonwealths, churches and schools. This is especially so if it is rightly joined, as is fitting, with sacred Theology; then it offers hospitality and patronage to all the arts and disciplines, to all honest trades and crafts, to schools and churches. How useful and salutary, then, it is to have well-ordered polities and commonwealths, prudently constituted in the right form of government; to have good magistrates, councils and senates, courts of justice and laws; to have schools and churches, arts and disciplines of every kind, both philosophical and mechanical; and finally to have good citizens, craftsmen and workmen. So useful and salutary too is practical or political Philosophy.

units.la: Inter alias vero, easque innumeras ipsius vtilitates, hæc quoque non postrema est, quod ad præstantissimas omnium & nobilissimas Facultates ac Scientias, ad Theo-logiam, inquam, & imprimis ad Iurisprudentiam non pa-rum conducit. Etenim lex naturæ seu conscientiæ, honestique mores ac disciplina, salutares leges ac virtutes; hæc inquam, & alia complura, de quibus Ethica & Politica tra-ctat, decalogo, & vitæ piæ ac Christianæ quasi viam parant, aut certè non spernenda ad eandem illam media & organa existunt. Repeto & illud, quod paulò ante attigi, videlicet quòd viri ac magistratus politici, seu disciplina politica instructi, custodes ac patroni esse debent Ecclesiæ & religionis, custodes decalogi, custodes ac patroni studij Theologici, custodes scholarum, omniumque bonarum artium ac disciplinarum, præsertim divinarum. Id quod passim ac multoties ab Imperatore Iustiniano, in Codice, ac præsertim in Novellis plurimis, affirmatur & iteratur. Nec enim ulla politia rectè constituta & solidè fundata est; ubi vera religio, ac vera pietas non viget ac floret.
units.tr: Among its other, indeed countless, uses, this is not the least: it contributes not a little to the most excellent and noble of all the faculties and sciences, namely theology and, above all, jurisprudence. For the law of nature or of conscience, honourable morals and discipline, wholesome laws and virtues, and many other things with which Ethics and Politics deal, prepare the way, as it were, for the decalogue and for a godly and Christian life, or at least are no mean means and instruments towards that same end. I repeat also what I touched on a little earlier: that political men and magistrates, instructed in political discipline, ought to be the guardians and patrons of the Church and of religion, guardians of the decalogue, guardians and patrons of theological study, guardians of schools and of all the good arts and disciplines, especially the divine ones. The Emperor Justinian affirms and repeats this again and again in the Code, and especially in his many Novels. For no commonwealth is rightly constituted and soundly founded where true religion and true piety do not flourish.

units.la: Verumenimuero ad Iurisprudentiam tantum confert Politica: ut illa potius nil aliud reuera esse videatur, quàm ea, quæ antiquitus non Iurisprudentia, sed Politica dicebatur: aut certè nil aliud, quàm plenior quædam magisque practica & quasi exemplaris Politica. Prima sanè & intima Iurisprudentiæ, legum, magistratuum, iudiciorum, iustitiæ, iuris & æquitatis, principia & fundamenta, ex Philosophia Ethica & Politica dependent: Principium autem est potissima pars cuiusque rei, l.1.§.1.ff. de Origine iuris.
