Neque tamen principia duntaxat inde dependent: Sed infinitis modis ac partibus ambæ inter se conspirant, eademque tractant, & inter se quasi correspondent. Ac Iuris prudentia quidem non pauca à Philosophia, præsertim politica, mutuatur: Sectatur enim & affectat veram, non simulatâ Philosophiâ, l.1.ff. de iustitia & iure: Philosophia enim est res religiosa, & civilis seu politica sapientia est res sanctissima, ut dicitur l.1.ff. de extraordinariis cognitionib. Unde Divus Marcus Imperator tanquam Philosophiæ plenus laudatur, l.11.C. de his quibus ut indignis &c. Politica virtutem requirit, eamque præscribit & singulis & in Oeconomia, & in Politia consociatis. Leges Iurisprudentiæ & iustitia universalis similiter omnes virtutes & obedien-tiam erga easdem requirunt, & quidem ipso actu seu praxi expressam obedientiam : quam etiam præmiis coronant, sicut inobedientiam contrà, præsertim enormem, pœnis. Etenim bonos non solùm metu pœnarum, sed etiam præ-miorù exhortatione efficere cupiunt Iureconsulti, l.1. ff. de iustitia & iure. Nam præmia virtutum bene meritis tri-bui conuenit, l. 4. C. de statuis & imaginibus: & præmiis bene meriti prouocandi sunt,l. 1. C. pro quibus causis ser-ui & c. Pœnis verò non delectamur ( nihil enim nobis tam gratum est quàm humanitas) ait Imperator; & tamen cō-stituendæ & aliquando augendæ sunt pœnæ,vt earum me-tu eos , qui ad peccandum procliues sunt, à peccando ar-ceamus,l.57. C. de episcopis & clericis. Politica non rigi-dè vrget verba legis, sed mentem, sensum & interpreta-tionem quærit. Iurisprudentia idem facit : leges enim sci-re, non est verba earum tenere, sed vim ac potestatem: & leges benigniùs interpretandæ sunt, vt voluntas earum conseruetur,l. 17. & 18.ff. de legibus. Illa æquitatem sæpius desiderat: Hæc eandem creberrimè flagitat: placuit enim in omnibus rebus præcipuam esse æquitatis potiùs, quàm strictiiuris rationem.l. 8. C. de iudiciis. Neque vlla iuris ratio patitur, vt quæ salubriter pro vtilitate hominum in-troducùtur, ea nos duriore interpretatione producamus ad seueritatem,l. 25.ff. de legibus: nam in omnibus qui-dem, sed maximè tamen in iure, spectanda est æquitas, l. 90. ff. de regulis iuris.Illa de iure & iustitia multa præcipit: Sed hæc certè non pauciora. Iurisprudentiæ nanque pri-mordia & primi tum in Institutionibus,tum in Digestis ti-tuli de iustitia & iure, de origine iuris , de iure naturali, gentium & ciuili inchoantur. Illa de repub. deque com-modis publicis, de magistratibus, curiis & senatibus, de iurisdictione , ac iudiciis,& similibus, multa præcipit: sed hæc certè longè plura : in quibus ipsis tamen principia & fundamenta politica studiosè consecatur. Verù de his omnibus Clarissimum ac Præstantissimum virum D. D. Iulium Pacium inter Iureconsultos ævi huius Philosophiæ ac Politicæ peritissimum, inter Philosophos ac Politicos iure consultissimū, & alterum huius ætatis Papinianū pro perspicacissimo ingenio & exquisitissimo iudicio suo, perorare, ac perorante audire malim: præsertim cum sentiam, mihi nunc ad alia properandum esse & fastigiū huic orationi imponendum.
units.tr: Yet political philosophy contributes so much to jurisprudence that the former seems in truth to be nothing other than what was once called not jurisprudence but politics, or at least a fuller and more practical, and as it were exemplary, politics. Certainly the first and innermost principles and foundations of jurisprudence (of laws, magistrates, judgments, justice, right and equity) depend on ethical and political philosophy; for the principle is the chief part of anything, l.1.§.1.ff. de Origine iuris. Nor do the principles alone depend on it. In countless ways and parts the two agree with each other, handle the same matters, and correspond with one another as it were. Jurisprudence borrows not a few things from philosophy, especially political philosophy: for it pursues and aims at true philosophy, not feigned philosophy, l.1.ff. de iustitia & iure; for philosophy is a sacred matter, and civil or political wisdom is a most holy thing, as stated in l.1.ff. de extraordinariis cognitionib. Hence the divine Emperor Marcus is praised as one full of philosophy, l.11.C. de his quibus ut indignis &c. Politics requires virtue and prescribes it both to individuals and to those united in household and commonwealth. The laws of jurisprudence and universal justice likewise require all virtues and obedience towards themselves, and indeed an obedience expressed in the very act or practice; they crown it with rewards, just as they punish disobedience, especially gross disobedience, with penalties. For jurists desire to make men good not only by fear of punishments but also by the encouragement of rewards, l.1.ff. de iustitia & iure. For it is fitting that rewards of virtue be given to the well deserving, l.4.C. de statuis & imaginibus; and those who have deserved well are to be stirred up by rewards, l.1.C. pro quibus causis servi &c. "We do not, however, take delight in punishments (for nothing is so pleasing to us as humanity)," says the Emperor; and yet punishments must be established, and sometimes increased, so that by fear of them we may keep from sin those who are prone to sinning, l.57.C. de episcopis et clericis. Politics does not cling rigidly to the words of the law, but seeks its mind, sense and interpretation. Jurisprudence does the same: for to know the laws is not to hold their words but their force and power; and laws are to be interpreted more kindly, so that their will may be preserved, l.17. & 18.ff. de legibus. The one often requires equity; the other requests it very often. For it has been decided that in all matters equity is to be preferred to the strict reasoning of the law, l.8.C. de iudiciis. Nor does any principle of law allow that what is wisely introduced for the benefit of men should be drawn by us, through a harsher interpretation, into severity, l.25.ff. de legibus; for equity is to be regarded in all things, but most of all in law, l.90.ff. de regulis iuris. The one commands much about right and justice; but the other certainly commands no fewer things. For the beginnings and first elements of jurisprudence, both in the Institutes and in the Digest, begin with the titles on justice and right, on the origin of law, and on natural, international and civil law. The one commands much about the commonwealth, public goods, magistrates, courts and senates, jurisdiction and judgments, and similar matters; but the other certainly commands far more, and in these very matters it diligently pursues the political principles and foundations. But on all these matters I would rather have the most distinguished and excellent man, D. D. Julius Pacius, the most skilled in philosophy and politics among the jurists of this age, and among philosophers and politicians the most learned in law, and a second Papinian of our time, speak and be heard, on account of his keen mind and most exact judgment. Especially since I perceive that I must now hasten to other matters and put a crown on this oration.

units.la: Quanta sit ergo totius Philosophiæ Politicæ in tanta humanæ vitæ miseria, non iucunditas nunc dicam aut dignitas, sed utilitas dicam: imò necesitas: Id verò experientia ipsa facile confirmat, hominum inter homines societas abundè declarat, & communis mortalium vita perspicuè demonstrat: singulorum conscientiæ tacitè fatentur, sed res œconomicæ aperte loquuntur, & politicæ manifestè testantur.
units.tr: How great, then, is the whole of political philosophy amid such great misery of human life? I shall speak not now of its pleasantness or dignity, but of its usefulness; indeed of its necessity. Experience itself easily confirms this; the society of men among men declares it abundantly, and the common life of mortals demonstrates it plainly. The consciences of individuals tacitly confess it, economic affairs speak it openly, and the affairs of the commonwealth clearly bear witness to it.

units.la: Præclarè itaque Socrates apud Xenophontem: Generosum est & omni fauore dignum ingenium, cui sunt cordi disciplinæ politicæ: Egregiè ille, quisquis est, in dialogo de Philosophia apud Platonem: Ego verò (inquit) ô Socrates, si istam Philosophiā, Politicā scilicet imprimis, turpe esse ducerem, ne hominis quidē appellatione dignus essem; nec ego, nec alius quisquam, malè de ea sentiens. Etenim politica & Ethica, omnia omnium hominum studia liberalia, & officia honesta complectitur ac moderatur, & in universas totius humanæ vitæ partes quàm latissimè diffunditur. Hæc non tantùm de singulorum, sed simul etiam plurium & omniù, seu in œconomia seu in politia degentium, vita, moribus, educationibus, institutionibus, muneribus & operibus, factis & actionibus, præmiis & pœnis præcipit. Hæc totius Philosophiæ ac literarum & disciplinarum omniù ad commodam huius vitæ sustentationem, ac politicà prosperitatem comparata praxis quædam & finis existit.
units.tr: Socrates, in Xenophon, says it nobly: a mind that is devoted to political disciplines is noble and deserving of every favour. In Plato's dialogue on philosophy, whoever he is speaks admirably: "But I, O Socrates," he says, "if I thought that philosophy, political philosophy above all, was shameful, would not even be worthy of the name of man; nor do I, or anyone else, think ill of it." For politics and ethics embrace and govern all the liberal pursuits and honourable duties of all men, and spread as widely as possible into all parts of human life. They prescribe for the life, morals, upbringing, instruction, duties and works, deeds and actions, rewards and punishments not only of individuals but at the same time of many and of all, whether they live in a household or in a commonwealth. This is a certain practice and end of the whole of philosophy, of all letters and disciplines, prepared for the convenient sustaining of this life and for political prosperity.

units.la: Hæc, ut pulcherrimè Aristoteles loquitur, omnium artium maximè est ἀρχιτεκτονική[?]. Huic nimirum, velut architectatrici, omnes disciplinæ subiectæ sunt atque laborant.
units.tr: This, as Aristotle most finely puts it, is the most architectonic [ἀρχιτεκτονική] of all the arts. To it, as to a kind of architect, all the disciplines are subject and labour.

units.la: Enimverò cuncta opificia honesta, omnes artes ac facultates liberales, universæ leges & constitutiones laudabiles, politiæ, seu politicæ hominum congregationi ac societati, hoc est publicæ hominum utilitati & prosperitati inseruire & accommodari, ac vicissim à magistratibus & viris politicis, regi, foueri, & conseruari debent. Ad sum-mam: Politica & Ethica non solùm homines primùm om-nium inter se politicè ac rectè consociauit & conciliauit, sed etiam omnis generis bona, tum externa (seu mobilia, seu immobilia, seu naturalia, seu arte & studio parta) tum interna, tum priuata, tum publica, tum corporis, tum a-nimi, tum virtutes, tum artes, seu Philosophicas seu me-chanicas, adeoque cuncta ad politicam hominum inter homines (tum aliquorum, tum plurium, aut vniuersorum) societatem tuendam, ad familias constituendas, ad Res-pub. constabiliendas, ad ciuilem & externam honestatem conseruandam, adeoque ad communem huius vitæ susté-tationem, tranquillitatem & prosperitatem procurandâ, necessaria bona primum inquisiuit atque præscripsit: Po-liticosque viros suas œconomias, & politias, istis ipsis bo-nis instruere, fouereque atque firmare docuit ac præcepit; hodieque etiamnû docet ac præcipit. Itaque hæ disciplinæ rectè traditæ, metam ac finem nostrorum studiorum, la-borum & actionum demonstrant: Nempe ad Dei gloriam, & ad communem hominum societatem, pacem ac felici-tatem, omnia referenda esse. Hæ primos fontes, princi-pia ac demonstrationes, iustitiæ & iurisprudentiæ, legum æquitatis ac iudiciorum aperiunt: hæ legem naturæ expo-nunt, discrimen honesti ac turpis ostendunt: Præmia ho-neste viuentibus decernunt, poenas malè agentibus con-stituunt. Et vt medicina corpus, sic Ethica animum sanat: vel potius vtrumque curat. Vt homo per cæteras artes res extra se positas, sic per Ethicam semetipsum cognoscit: vt per agriculturam agros: sic per Ethicam se ipsum colit. Quamobrem Ethices ac politices vsus, non minor inter homines est, quàm panis, aquæ, aëris & solis: Dignitas autem multò etiam præstantior. Non enim hoc spectat solùm, vt nutriantur ac foueantur, id est, vt viuant, & quidem vnâ simul viuant homines, sed etiam vt piè, tran-quillè, honestè, commodè ac prosperè viuant. Rectè itaque cum M. Tullio exclamare nobis licebit, auditores: ô Philosophia Ethica ac Politica, unica vitæ, post Theologiam, dux, ô virtutis indagatrix, expultrixque vitiorum: quid non modo nos sed omnino quid vita hominum sine te esse posset, &c. Tu mederis animis, cupiditatibus & affectibus liberas, &c. Huic itaque tam laudabili disciplinæ, Auditores, tam salutari medicinæ, nos demus excolendos; ab hac patiamur nos, secundum Theologiam, sanari: hinc adiumenta & consilia prosperè viuendi petamus.
units.tr: Indeed, all honourable crafts, all liberal arts and faculties, all laudable laws and constitutions, and commonwealths or the politics of human gathering and society ought to serve and be adapted to the good and prosperity of men, that is, to public human utility, and in turn ought to be ruled, cherished and preserved by magistrates and political men. In sum: politics and ethics not only first of all joined and united men together among themselves politically and rightly, but also first sought out and prescribed all kinds of goods, both external (whether movable or immovable, whether natural or acquired by skill and effort), and internal, both private and public, both of the body and of the mind, both virtues and arts, whether philosophical or mechanical; and so all the goods necessary for preserving the political society of men among men (of some, of many, or of all), for establishing families, for stabilising commonwealths, for preserving civil and external honesty, and for procuring the common sustenance, tranquillity and prosperity of this life. And it taught and commanded political men to furnish, cherish and strengthen their households and commonwealths with these very goods; and it still teaches and commands this today. Therefore these disciplines, rightly handed down, show the goal and end of our studies, labours and actions: namely, that all things are to be referred to the glory of God and to the common society, peace and happiness of men. They open the first sources, principles and demonstrations of justice and jurisprudence, of laws, equity and judgments; they set out the law of nature and show the difference between the honourable and the shameful; they decree rewards for those who live honourably and establish penalties for those who act badly. And as medicine heals the body, so ethics heals the mind; or rather, it cares for both. As man knows the things placed outside himself through the other arts, so through ethics he knows himself; as he tends the fields through agriculture, so through ethics he tends himself. Wherefore the use of ethics and politics is no less among men than bread, water, air and sun; and its dignity is far more excellent still. For this concerns not only that men be nourished and cherished, that is, that they live, and indeed live together, but also that they live piously, quietly, honourably, comfortably and prosperously. Therefore, listeners, we may rightly exclaim with Marcus Tullius: "O philosophy of ethics and politics, the sole guide of life after theology, O investigator of virtue and expeller of vices: what could not only we but the life of men altogether be without you, etc.? You heal the mind, freeing it from desires and passions, etc." Therefore, listeners, let us give ourselves to cultivate this so praiseworthy a discipline, this so wholesome a medicine; let us allow ourselves, next to theology, to be healed by it; from it let us seek the aids and counsels of living well.

units.la: Sed longius excurrit oratio, quàm instituera m. Ha-ctenus ergo proœmium & quasi προαύλιον[?] actus nostri fuit: Nunc porrò quod restat agamus: hoc est, ad ipsam Pro-motionē ac renunciationem sensim propiùs accedamus. Itaque accedo tandem ad id, ob quod præcipuè & hic con-ventus est institutus, & ego cum hisce Candidatis, in has cathedras conscendere sum iussus. Quod ergo felix fau-stumque sit, ego ea autoritate, quæ mihi hoc tempore publicè est attributa, ex decreto Collegii Philosophici (quod etiam communi totius Academiæ consensu est ap-probatum) vos novem honestissimos & eruditissimos juvenes & universos & singulos, Te Ioannem Krejum Hachenburgensem: VVolfgangum Lostium Bornensem Misenum: Ioannem Fridericum Schlöer Lutræum: Ioannem Cneffelium Freistadiensem Silesium: Regnerum Hachtingum Göningensem Frisium: Regnerum Gruterum Daventriensem: Balthasarum Rhot Grunbergensem Silesium: VVigandum VValtherum Obernhofensem VVetteraujum: Casparum Scultetum Greiffenbergensem Silesium: vos, inquam, & universos & singulos, Licentiatos libera-lium artium paulò ante renunciatos, nunc etiam Philoso-phiæ Doctores (quos Magistros appellamus) quàm pos-[?]ium iure & forma optima creo, renuntio & saluto, vosque tales ab aliis quoque haberi & salutari hac publica & solenni renunciatione cupio: vobisque ea omnia iura & cōmoda, quæ vel legibus vel laudata consuetudine, liberaliū artium magistris antiquitus sunt attributa, pro vestris meritis tribuo & concedo. Sed interim vos moneo & quaeso, vt Philosophorum monumenta sedulò & accurate legere pergatis: Vtque in ea studia, in quæ iam estis feliciter ingressi, & in quæ deinceps ingressuri, assiduè & alacriter, sed non sine inuocato Dei numine (quod & facitis) incubatis; vt nimirum & vobis honori, & vestris laudi, & (quod caput rei est) Ecclesiæ Christi ac reipub. vsui esse queatis. Id quod Iehoua propter Christum per Spiritum Sanctum faxit Ex animo igitur vobis hoc modo gratulor
units.tr: But my speech has run on longer than I intended. So far, then, this has been the preface and, as it were, the forecourt [προαύλιον] of our act. Now let us do what remains and move gradually closer to the promotion and proclamation itself. I come at last to the matter for which this assembly has chiefly been convened, and for which I have been ordered to mount these chairs with these candidates. So, may it be fortunate and auspicious: by the authority that has been publicly conferred on me at this time, and by decree of the Philosophical Faculty (which has also been approved by the common consent of the whole University), I create, proclaim and greet you, nine most honourable and learned young men, both all together and each one individually: Johannes Krejus of Hachenburg; Wolfgang Lostius of Borna in Meissen; Johannes Friedrich Schlöer of Lauter; Johannes Cneffelius of Freistadt in Silesia; Regnerus Hachtingus of Göningen in Friesland; Regnerus Gruterus of Deventer; Balthasar Rhot of Grünberg in Silesia; Wigand Walther of Obernhofen in the Wetterau; Caspar Scultetus of Greiffenberg in Silesia: you, I say, all and each, who were lately proclaimed Licentiates of the liberal arts, I now also create Doctors of Philosophy (whom we call Masters) with the best right and form. I wish you to be regarded and greeted as such by others too, through this public and solemn proclamation. And to you I assign and grant, according to your merits, all those rights and privileges which, by law or by long-established custom, have from antiquity belonged to masters of the liberal arts. Meanwhile I advise and beg you to keep diligently and carefully reading the monuments of the philosophers, and to apply yourselves constantly and eagerly to those studies which you have now happily entered upon, and which you will enter hereafter, yet not without calling on the power of God (as indeed you do), so that you may be an honour to yourselves, a credit to your own praise and, what is the main point, of use to the Church of Christ and the commonwealth. May Jehovah grant this, for the sake of Christ, through the Holy Spirit. With all my heart I congratulate you in this way.

units.la: ἐκ [?]μεσσᾶν ζαθέου θνητοὶ κλέος αἰεὶ κιχῶσι[?] / τῶν [?]κλειτῶν μέσυν ἀθάνατον σοφίαν [?]&c.
units.tr: Mortals always win fame from the midst of the sacred... of the famous men, immortal wisdom... [ἐκ μεσσᾶν ζαθέου θνητοὶ κλέος αἰεὶ κιχῶσι / τῶν κλειτῶν μέσυν ἀθάνατον σοφίαν &c.]

units.la: Sed quoniâ ita comparatū & receptum esse sentio, vt præ-ter hanc iam peractam honoris Philosophici renuntiatio-nem, in his Academicis ac panegyricis concentibus etiâ externi quidam ritus ac ceremoniæ, quibus hoc Philosophicum Magisterium quasi sigillis & arrhis quibusdam muniturac sancitur; adhibeantur: Nos quoque hanc tum in hac tum in aliis Academiis receptam consuetudinem sequemur. Itaque primum omnium vos in hanc honestis-simam & altissimam cathedram ascendere iubeo: Idque propterea, vt sciatis, vos deinceps obscuros latere nec posse nec debere, sed futuros posthac plures, quàm antea, qui mores, studia, vitamque vestram totam obseruent: Et idcirco sedulam vobis operam dandam esse, vt doctrina prudentia & vitæ innocentia aliis præluceatis. Secundò pileum hunc libertatis olim indicem & symbolum, capiti vestro impono: qui vos commonefaciat, ne voluptatibus & cupiditatibus illiberalibus vos seruiliter mancipetis: Neque Philosophicam in afferenda veritate libertatem negligatis. Tertiò digitis vestris hos annulos aureos induco, vt intelligatis, nouam hanc honoris nobilitatem, vt virtute & doctrina parta est: sic virtute & doctrina conseruandam & amplificandam esse: ac veritatem Philosophicâ tan-
units.tr: But since I understand that it is the custom and accepted practice that, besides this already completed proclamation of philosophical honour, certain external rites and ceremonies also be employed in these academic and festive proceedings, by which this Philosophical Mastership is, as it were, secured and sanctioned with seals and pledges, we too shall follow this custom, which is observed both here and in other universities. First of all, then, I bid you ascend this most honourable and lofty chair. I do so that you may know that from now on you can and should not remain obscure, but that many more than before will observe your conduct, your studies and your whole life. Therefore you must take care to shine as examples to others by your learning, prudence and innocence of life. Second, I place on your head this cap, once the sign and emblem of liberty, to remind you not to surrender yourselves in servile fashion to pleasures and ignoble desires, and not to neglect the philosophical freedom of asserting the truth. Third, I put these golden rings on your fingers, so that you may understand that this new nobility of honour, just as it has been won by virtue and learning, must likewise be preserved and increased by virtue and learning; and that the truth of philosophy [is to be embraced] as a most chaste virgin and bride, and that you, as bridegrooms, should plight yourselves to her with this betrothal ring, so that you always embrace her.

units.la: Reliqua enim carmina studiose hic omissa sunt. tanquam castissimam virginē & sponsam, vobis tanquam sponsis, isthoc annulo sponsalitio desponderi, vt eam semper amplectamini, & quantum in vobis esse potest, tueamini. Quartò & postremò hos vobis libros, tanquam praecipua armamenta & instrumenta scholastica, de manu in manum trado: primùm quidem apertos, vt sciatis, vos quae vera ac salutaria didicistis, candidè & apertè cum aliis communicare debere: Deinde eosdem etiā clausos vobis trado: vt intelligatis, quia memoria custos est rerum omnium lectione ac meditatione cognitarum, vobis in toto studiorum vestrorum curriculo memoriae imprimis sedulam & assiduam habendam esse curam: Ne videlicet in solis duntaxat libris sapiatis, sed vt etiam sine librorum adminiculo, cùm tempus flagitat, ea quae antea ex libris haustis, memoriae firmiter infixa & rectè intellecta, promptè & sine haesitatione in apricum proferre, animique sensa perspicuè cum audientium fructu, & vestra ipsorum laude explicare queatis.
units.tr: (The remaining verses have been deliberately omitted here.) Fourth and last, I hand over to you these books, as the chief tools and instruments of your schooling: first, indeed, open, so that you may know that what you have learned as true and salutary you ought to share with others frankly and openly; and then I hand them over to you closed as well, so that you may understand that, since memory is the guardian of all things learned by reading and meditation, you must take especial and constant care of your memory throughout the whole course of your studies. Namely, so that you may be wise not merely in books, but so that, even without the help of books, when the occasion demands, you can bring forth promptly and without hesitation what you have drunk in from books before, firmly fixed in memory and rightly understood, and can explain the thoughts of your minds clearly, to the profit of your hearers and to your own praise.

units.la: His omnibus, Dei benignitate, feliciter peractis: Restabat tandem, vt vos noui iam Doctores & Philosophiae Magistri, pro recepto in hac Academia more, singuli vestrae eruditionis, & ad alios docendum aptitudinis, vestraeq; in explicandis doctorum hominum & Philosophorum scriptis industriae ac dexteritatis, in hoc tam augusto, honesto & iucundo praestantissimorum virorum coetu, specimen aliquod in hac cathedra ederetis. Sed ne tam frequentis & honorifici Clarissimorū virorum confessus, & florentissimae lectissimorum iuuenum coronae patientia abutamur, age, tu D.M. Caspare Scultete Philosophicae huic & panegyricae Festiuitati debita & conueniente gratiarum actione optatum finem imponito.
units.tr: With all these things happily accomplished, by God's goodness, it remained finally that you, now newly Doctors and Masters of Philosophy, should, according to the custom received in this Academy, each give from this chair some specimen of your learning, of your aptitude for teaching others, and of your industry and skill in explaining the writings of learned men and philosophers, in this so august, honourable and pleasant gathering of most distinguished men. But lest we abuse the patience of this so numerous and honourable assembly of most illustrious men, and of this flourishing crown of the most select young men, come now, you, Master Caspar Scultetus, bring to a close the desired end, with a thanksgiving fitting and due to this philosophical and festive occasion.
To God alone be glory [μόνῳ τῷ θεῷ δόξα].
